Headline: Warning after battery sparks bin lorry fire in Glasgow
Body:
Residents have been urged to recycle batteries properly after a bin lorry went on fire on a busy Glasgow city centre street.

Waste from the lorry had to be unloaded onto the city's Jamaica Street on Wednesday morning after crews realised the truck was alight.

It is believed to be the eighth fire like this so far this year.

Glasgow City Council said it was "vital" that people recycle their batteries properly, and did not put them into general waste.

GMB trade union convenor Chris Mitchell described the incident – which happened at about 07:50 - as a "warning".

"We are just one fire away from a disaster to be honest," he said.

"Everyone has a responsibility to put the proper materials in the bins when they are emptying their rubbish.

"We are unsure where the electrical goods came from but the fire started after the bins at the student accommodation were emptied.

"I would urge people to be mindful of what they are putting in these bins, especially electrical goods. We have fantastic commercial and bulk uplift or recycling centres where it can be disposed of safely."

Glasgow City Council said the incident highlighted the dangers linked to battery disposal.

A spokesperson said: "It is vital that we all take care to recycle batteries properly.

"Batteries can be safely recycled at a wide range of shops or at any of our household waste recycling centres.

"Staff followed the correct procedure by unloading the waste in the vehicle as soon as they became aware of the fire. This quick response ensured they were unharmed and minimised the risk of damage to the vehicle."

Story by Local Democracy Reporting Service reporter Catherine Hunter.

Headline: Memories of rock royalty in my garden in Knebworth
Body:
Not many people can say Queen and Oasis have played in their back garden. Henry Lytton Cobbold can.

Forty years ago, on 9 August 1986, Freddie Mercury, Brian May, Roger Taylor and John Deacon brought Queen's sold-out European tour to a close at Knebworth House in Hertfordshire.

Lytton Cobbold, now the owner of the estate, was 24 at the time and remembers the suitably rock-and-roll celebrations backstage afterwards, complete with fairground rides and naked women mud wrestling.

"They had a lot to celebrate," he recalls. "They'd really smashed it live the year before... And then of course it became legendary for various rather sadder reasons."

Five years later, Mercury died from bronchial pneumonia resulting from AIDS. His performance in front of 125,000 people at Knebworth was his final time on stage with Queen.

Lytton Cobbold says: "He was at the top of his game and nobody knew about his illness at that point.

"The other thing, of course, that makes it legendary is this bizarre fact that although the field was full of screens nobody pressed record.

"The only record we've got of the show is a little bit of news footage from the beginning and then a really bizarre bootleg that a Dutch guy took on his little home video camera of a screen at the back of the audience.

"I mean, imagine going to a Freddie Mercury gig and spending the whole time at the back of the audience filming the screen with your wobbly video camera."

Lytton Cobbold never met the band, unlike some of the other stars who had played Knebworth in earlier years.

"Back in the old days, they didn't used to helicopter off the minute they'd done the encore, they would come up and chill at the house until the roads cleared."

Knebworth Park has hosted live music since 1974. Pink Floyd were the first major act to play the venue in 1975, with the Rolling Stones following a year later.

He said: "My mum and dad generally loved a party.

"I mean my dad's birthday was on 14 July, and every summer holiday began with a big party and the concerts just gave us that encore party. "

Genesis, Led Zeppelin, The Beach Boys and Cliff Richard were among the names to play Knebworth in the 1970s and 80s, but it was the 90s when guitars in Hertfordshire were heard around the world.

There was a lot happening in the UK in the summer of 1996: England hosted Euro 96, the Spice Girls made their debut, Dolly the sheep was cloned, and Oasis played two nights at Knebworth to 250,000 people.

"Our catering company did the bars in 96 and that was one of our biggest trading days ever... Quite a lot of beer was drunk that day," he recalls.

The band slept backstage in Winnebagos. Then, on the Monday morning, a dishevelled Noel Gallagher appeared at the back door.

Lytton Cobbold says: "We've got a four poster bath as part of our main guest room, our old Tudor guest room, and so my dad brought him a bottle of champagne in the bath.

"Subsequently in interviews he said that he was brought champagne by a liveried servant- it was actually my dad!"

Oasis only released recordings from those shows in recent years, but their Knebworth legacy has stayed strong.

Two turrets attached to the house, named Noel and Liam, were built using income from the 1996 shows.

Lytton Cobbold said: "The rest of this house is still falling down and you know, we've got massive repairs and bills still to pay to to do the rest of the house.

"So, we do need them to come back and help us fix the rest of the roof!"

Earlier this week, SJM Concerts, the promoter behind Oasis' 2025 reunion, was granted a licence to host large events at Knebworth .

However Lytton Cobbold insists "there is nothing set yet".

He adds: "I'm confident that Oasis will play Knebworth again, and I would love it to be next year, I would love it to be whenever they want to come, whenever feels right for them."

When asked if it would be fitting to announce a return on Monday, the 30th anniversary of their Knebworth shows, he agrees, but says his wife handles bookings and he does not know what is planned.

"They have got a documentary coming out in September and they'll want to make a bit of buzz around their documentary. If they want to make some announcements, I would have thought that would be more of the time to do it.

"We're delighted that our local authorities are supporting the licence, that's great, fingers crossed that all comes together, but it's not happening as of today."

Headline: Man guilty of harassing MP Stella Creasy on Tube train
Body:
A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP for Walthamstow after preventing her from leaving a Tube carriage and behaving in an "abusive and aggressive" manner.

Clifford Wilby, from east London, targeted Stella Creasy on a Victoria line train between Walthamstow Central and Finsbury Park on 15 July last year.

Westminster Magistrates' Court heard how Wilby spoke to Creasy about knife crime and her "failings as a Member of Parliament" before filming her, leading to members of the public intervening.

Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

Wilby and Creasy first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 as part of her role as an MP.

She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else's case.

Creasy said he had "made a series of very serious allegations", became abusive and "referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath".

The meeting was stopped because of Wilby's behaviour.

On 15 July last year, Creasy made eye contact with Wilby on a Victoria line train.

She told the court: "He stood up and blocked my ability to leave the carriage. He began talking to me about his concerns about my constituent. He was shouting, although the Tube train is a loud environment."

She added: "Obviously I was concerned that I was in an enclosed space with him. He was very close.

"I stated very clearly this wasn't an appropriate conversation to be having."

The MP said she was backed against the carriage doors and holding her hands out as a gesture "to say stop".

Passengers stepped in, with one man positioning himself between her and the defendant.

"I was worried that because Mr Wilby was escalating, he could turn his attention and his aggression to the other people on the train trying to protect me," she said.

A woman also told Wilby to stop, saying his behaviour amounted to harassment, and encouraged Creasy to sit next to her.

Creasy left the train at Finsbury Park through a different set of doors after she believed other passengers had distracted him.

Wilby told the court he had hoped to continue their previous conversation about the constituent on the Tube, but claimed Creasy "became quite agitated" and that he was "quite shocked by her reaction".

He said he started recording on his phone "for my safety".

Wilby denied standing in front of Creasy and claimed she spoke to him first. He also denied telling her in 2024 that he had been diagnosed as a psychopath.

Delivering his verdict, Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram referred to footage in which Wilby said: "I don't care about your feelings, your feelings don't matter to me".

He added: "She made her own position very clear. She said that 'I repeatedly asked him to stop, he didn't, he was abusive and aggressive' and it's clear from the defendant's own words he did not care.

"In relation to the conduct of the two members of the public who intervened, the situation must have been such that there was concern for her safety, otherwise they would clearly not have intervened as they did."

Wilby is due to be sentenced on 8 September.

Headline: PM admits cost of living help is not enough and hints at further support
Body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he accepts his announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Burnham told BBC's Wake up to Money he will deliver an "accumulation of smaller things" that "combine to take the pressure down" on household budgets.

He spoke of an overhaul of train fares and "more public control" of energy, water and housing but did not give details on how he would bring this about.

Burnham has made a number of announcements to help people with the cost of living since taking office, including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to 'subscription traps' .

Asked whether the changes he had announced were not significant to people struggling, he said: "I can accept criticism that this isn't enough, because I wouldn't say it's enough.

"But I take an approach to politics where I do what I can, when I can. Just take that little bit of pressure off and address an issue that you know needs addressing.

"It's not the end of the story," he added.

The prime minister, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, said he believed "more public control of essential services" such as water, energy and housing, "would mean we could get to a more substantial answer to the cost of living crisis".

On water, he said it would not be easy to reverse the privatisation of water companies in England and Wales that took place in the 1980s.

"But very much, I'm looking at what can be done. Same with energy."

He also said that, following the return of rail operators to public ownership, he wanted to "remodel the rail fares so that we can get more public benefit for people".

It comes as the government said on Wednesday that people living within 1,600ft (500m) of new upgraded electricity pylons and substations across Britain will receive a £250 annual discount on their bills for a decade.

Burnham told the BBC he has asked Chancellor John Healey to look at what the government can do further on the cost of living in the upcoming Budget, on 28 October, and that Healey has said it will be his "main focus".

Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.

One major think tank recently warned that he will have to raise taxes or cut spending to meet Burnham's pledges on defence and the cost of living.

Labour's manifesto pledge was to not increase taxes for working people — including income tax, VAT and National Insurance Contributions (NICs) - which Burnham has said he will uphold.

He will likely face pressure to address rising costs for businesses, after previous budgets under Rachel Reeves saw employer's national insurance and minimum wages go up.

Last month Burnham said pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England would be given a 20% cut to business rates from April, calling it a "first step" to help the industry.

He told the BBC he accepted the national insurance hike had added pressure on businesses, and that the government would look at business rates "more broadly".

Burnham said: "I would like to bring down the cost of doing businesses. I want to make high streets more vibrant across the country. I know that cannot be done by simply wishing it."

But he said he did not want to "at this point, start making commitments".

"Those are for the Budget."

Headline: 30 years later, a former gang member will stand trial for Tupac's murder
Body:
It's been three decades filled with mystery, conspiracies - and anger.

The drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 changed the trajectory of hip-hop and elevated the rapper from the face of the genre to a cultural icon.

His killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023, when Duane "Keffe D" Davis was unexpectedly charged with murdering the famous rapper.

The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He's pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he faces life in prison without parole.

The trial is likely to unravel the intricacies of the bitter and deadly East Coast vs West Coast rap rivalries and turf wars between the Bloods and the Crips street gangs that were immortalised in rap lyrics and news reports in the 1990s.

It could also include several celebrity witnesses - including Suge Knight, the former CEO of Death Row Records, who has been thought of as the last surviving witness to Shakur's death.

But the complicated case hinges almost exclusively on one key piece of evidence: a book co-authored by Davis that he has argued is partially a piece of fiction.

Jury selection in the case began on Monday, with opening arguments due to start on 17 August.

To understand how the case became so mythologised, you have to go back to rivalries that grew larger than the men at its centre.

In the Los Angeles gang landscape of the 1990s, there was a vicious turf war between the Bloods, often represented by the colour red, and Crips, who often wore blue.

But that territorial dispute spread through the airwaves as part of a bigger national rivalry - East Coast v West Coast rap. The genre dispute was represented by two rival record companies that defined 1990s hip-hop: Knight's Death Row Records and Sean "Diddy" Combs' Bad Boy Records.

"The funny thing about it is Tupac is actually an East Coast rapper," said Jeff Pearlman, author of Only God Can Judge Me: The Many Lives of Tupac Shakur.

Born in New York City, Tupac moved to northern California as a teenager. He became known as a southern California rapper after signing with Death Row Records, which included acts like Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre.

Santi Elijah Holley, author of An Amerikan Family: The Shakurs and the Nation They Created, says the Death Row persona never told the whole story.

Tupac's mother Afeni was a Black Panther and he grew up around the black liberation movement. Holley says his music became his politics: "His activism was his art, his lyrics."

He acted in a number of Hollywood movies, and released hip-hop's first double album, All Eyez on Me, which sold over 5,000,000 copies.

That album, which debuted months before his death, cemented his place in the cannon of gangsta rap, a genre that celebrated the violent life of street criminals and drug dealers.

After he was shot in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996, he became immortalised as a kind of martyr for the lifestyle he helped make famous.

That fatal night began when Tupac and Knight attended a boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon at the MGM Grand.

After the match, surveillance footage captured Tupac and members of his entourage, who police have said were associated the Mob Piru Bloods street gang, attacking a man named Orlando Anderson, an alleged member of the South Side Compton Crips.

About three hours after the attack, Tupac was riding in the passenger seat of Knight's BMW driving through Las Vegas when a white Cadillac pulled alongside them and opened fire.

Tupac was hit four times and died six days later.

For nearly three decades, the killing remained one of America's most famous unsolved murders. There is no single explanation why.

Las Vegas police have long said witnesses refused to co-operate. Members of Tupac's entourage said police initially treated them like suspects and failed to follow important leads.

Within weeks of the shooting, investigators had identified Anderson from the MGM footage and questioned him.

He denied involvement and was never charged; he was killed in an unrelated shooting in 1998.

Over the years, police say they pursued thousands of tips, but the case stalled amid disappearing witnesses, many of whom were also killed in gang-related shootings, limited physical evidence, and a street code that forbade co-operation with police.

It was years later when Anderson's uncle, Davis, started talking and according to police, blew the case wide open again.

It was ultimately the death of another legendary rapper that helped unravel Tupac's shooting death.

Months after Shakur was gunned down, Biggie Smalls, or the Notorious BIG, was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles.

Both rappers were the stars of their respective rival record labels - Shakur with Death Row Records and Biggie with Bad Boy Records.

Biggie's case has remained unsolved, with no arrests or suspects.

In the mid 2000s the Los Angeles Police Department reopened the investigation and spoke with Davis, who was at a party with Biggie before the fatal shooting.

While Davis said he didn't have information about Biggie's death, he did have knowledge of Tupac's case and shared that he was in the car when the rapper was shot and killed. He told police the information in exchange that he not be charged.

That deal stuck until years later, when Davis went public with his knowledge.

He co-authored a memoir in 2019 titled Compton Street Legend, that claimed he not only was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot, but he was also the person who "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat of the Cadillac.

He never claimed to be the person who opened fire.

Davis also elaborated on the shooting to the media, detailing information to reporters in interviews.

Las Vegas police said his public statements had "reinvigorated" the investigation.

Over the next couple of years they spent time corroborating Davis' account and then in 2023, searched his home and seized multiple computers, two tubs of photographs and a slew of Tupac-related material, including a Vibe magazine.

He was arrested later that year.

Prosecutors have alleged that Tupac's killing was in retaliation for the beating of Davis' nephew - Orlando Anderson - just hours before the shooting.

They claim that Davis was the architect of the crime, who ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further gang criminal conduct.

Nevada prosecutors argued that by publicly talking about what happened on the night of Tupac's death and writing a book where he claimed to have supplied the gun, Davis had broken the agreement he entered into with law enforcement.

A judge later sided with the prosecutor's argument, opening the door for Davis' arrest.

Davis and his defence team have argued that the book was co-authored and sections were embellished or fictionalised to make a profit, and they should not be viewed as direct admissions.

In an interview last week with a local TV news station, Davis denied being in Las Vegas when Tupac was killed and distanced himself from the memoir that lists him as an author.

"I did not write that book," Davis told Fox 5. "A ghost writer wrote that."

He also said he might take the stand and testify at his trial.

"If I have to, I will."

Trial attorney Shaun Kent told the BBC: "This is what makes this case so fascinating. The two biggest pieces of evidence against Keffe D came from Keffe D.

"Keffe D has the right to take the stand and say 'I made all this up. I lied to sell copies of the book. I lied to the police. I'm a liar but I did not murder Tupac.'"

Davis has also publicly stated multiple times that Bad Boy Records head Sean "Diddy" Combs had offered him $1m to kill Death Row Records rivals Tupac and Knight.

Combs is currently serving a 50-month prison sentence after being convicted for two counts of transportation for the purposes of prostitution in New York. He has repeatedly denied allegations that he was involved in Tupac's death.

Prosecutors have released a list of potential witnesses who could be called to testify, with over 200 names, including members of Tupac's family, former mayor of Las Vegas Oscar Goodman and former Los Angeles police Detective Greg Kading.

Prosecutors have also named Knight, although it's unclear if the rap impresario will testify, as he's previously said he would not.

"This would be huge as he has never offered law enforcement any information that would lead to the conviction of anyone," Kent said. "This trial is going to be a legal scholar's Super Bowl."

Headline: Lucy Davis urges women to check their breasts for cancer - here's how
Body:
Signs of breast cancer are not always a lump in the traditional sense, so what should you look for?

Actress Lucy Davis, who played Dawn Tinsley in the original UK version of the popular TV series The Office, has revealed she has incurable breast cancer .

On Instagram , the 53-year-old said it had spread to her bones and it was too late for chemo.

She added: "The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny."

Here's how to check yourself at home.

The NHS says to check your breasts or chest about once a month.

That helps you learn what looks and feels normal for you, making it easier to notice any abnormal changes.

Breasts can naturally look and feel a bit different at different phases of your menstrual cycle, and change a bit as you age.

Instead, pay attention to:

Look at your breasts or chest in a mirror to look for any changes. Start with your arms by your sides and then raise them up.

Feel around each breast or side of your chest in a circular motion all the way up to your collarbone and under each armpit. Use a mix of light and firmer pressure. Do not press so hard it hurts.

Feel around and over each nipple.

Headline: Car washes and vape shops can still sponsor skilled foreign workers despite visa changes
Body:
More than 1,900 small high street businesses including mini-marts, vape shops and car washes are licensed to sponsor foreign workers under a specialist scheme intended for high-earning individuals despite visa rules being tightened, BBC Verify has found.

The Home Office scheme allows registered employers to recruit workers from overseas who meet a certain skill level. The rules were tightened in July 2025 to restrict the scheme mostly to graduate-level employees who would be earning at least £41,700.

But a year on from the rule change, BBC Verify has found more than 1,500 grocery and convenience stores, 150 taxi operators, 100 barber shops, and dozens of car washes and vape shops are still on the register and able to sponsor people to apply for visas.

More than 100 of those businesses were added to the skilled worker sponsorship list after the rules were tightened. Being on the register does not mean applications for individual visas would be approved.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said on Thursday the government will "make sure that the rules are being properly enforced because we cannot have employers getting round the rules or finding different ways to deviate".

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review into the presence of vape shops, barbers and car washes on the skilled worker sponsor register two months ago, following concerns over the "potential misuse of the system". The Home Office said at the time that any businesses seeking to abuse the system would have their licences revoked.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "We have raised the skilled worker threshold and over 100 occupations are now ineligible for new skilled worker visas."

It is understood some of the companies that joined the register after the rules changed may have applied before they took effect. Some companies may have also remained on the register because they were approved before July 2025 or are sponsoring workers who were already in the UK.

There are more than 120,000 businesses with licences to sponsor skilled workers. The skilled worker scheme was introduced after Brexit for employers to recruit workers after EU free movement ended. Smaller firms must pay a £611 fee to apply to join the register while larger businesses, such as those with more than 50 staff, pay a fee of £1,682. Anyone can be visited by the UK Visas and Immigration service during the application process.

Until July last year, someone being hired from abroad could qualify for sponsorship if their qualifications met an A-Level or equivalent standard, as long as they were paid at least £38,700 in most cases. Since the rule change, non-graduate professions, such as shop managers, are no longer eligible to apply. There are also higher English-language skill requirements that were introduced in January this year.

The Home Office said there were 68,067 skilled worker visas granted in the 12 months to March this year - 29,745 to main applicants and 38,322 to their dependants - which is 30% lower than the year before. IT professionals were the most common type of people to be granted the visas, followed by those people working in finance, while the fall in approvals was mostly attributed to those in food preparation and hospitality trades no longer qualifying for the scheme.

Jobs including sales and retail assistants, taxi drivers and chauffeurs are currently listed by the government as ineligible for skilled worker visas, but there are some exemptions, such as bricklayers, carpenters or nursing assistants and other occupations where there is a shortage in the UK.

The Home Office revoked 3,299 licences in 2025 compared with 347 in 2023. Its register does not state how many certificates of sponsorship or visas have been issued for each business or what type of role it has hired for, but Home Office guidance states firms must offer genuine jobs that meet skill and salary rules, and only sponsor workers for eligible roles.

As businesses are only listed by name, it is not always clear what industry a company operates within. BBC Verify identified the more than 1,900 small high-street businesses that had retained a sponsorship licence by matching their names and locations to Companies House records and Google business listings to identify whether the mini marts, car washes and other small operations were on the list, and by analysing company names.

Around 1,700 of those were in England, more than 140 were in Scotland, over 80 were in Wales and just two were in Northern Ireland.

Separately, BBC Verify found 60 businesses on the register that had been fined for employing illegal workers between April 2024 and December 2025. They had been fined a combined £2.5m.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "Illegal working will not be accepted, and businesses who face two or more illegal working penalties of up to £60,000, or fail to pay a penalty the first time, will have their license to hire workers revoked."

Speaking about the visa rule change, Dr Madeleine Sumption, director of the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, said that if businesses were on the register before the rules changed, they can continue to employ people they had already sponsored. "But they can't now bring in a new person to do those jobs."

Toby Way, a lawyer at WestBridge Business Immigration which helps businesses apply to be sponsors, told BBC Verify that while most sponsorship approvals are legitimate, "We come across a lot of exaggeration and some downright lying about sponsored roles".

"Hotels and restaurants have been hit massively by the rule changes. They're now unable to sponsor a chef or a manager, but they might claim they need someone for marketing or book-keeping, because those roles are on the temporary shortage list," he said.

"We know the Home Office looks at the finances of the businesses now and whether their revenue or profit means they can pay the required salary."

Immigration lawyer Joanna Hunt of DAC Beachcroft said that it would be difficult for a high street shop to justify sponsorship at the degree level.

"Subject to a few exceptions, a job needs to be skilled to 'degree level' to allow a business to sponsor a worker to fill it and the Home Office will consider if the role fits with the type of business the sponsor operates. A high street shop may find this requirement difficult to demonstrate."
